express-core.md:
## Why it exists
A raw Node HTTP server gives you a request and a response, and nothing else. **Express** adds routing, a middleware pipeline and conventions, which is why it is still the most widely used Node web framework. Express 5 is the current major version and requires Node 18 or newer.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
Every request flows through a chain of functions in the order you register them. Each function can end the response, or call `next()` to pass control on. A function with **four** arguments `(err, req, res, next)` is an error handler and only runs when something fails.

## Worked example
```js
import express from 'express'
import helmet from 'helmet'
import cors from 'cors'
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit'
import { z } from 'zod'

const app = express()
app.set('trust proxy', 1)                          // behind a load balancer
app.use(helmet())                                   // security headers
app.use(cors({ origin: ['https://app.example.com'] }))
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }))
app.use(rateLimit({ windowMs: 60_000, limit: 100 }))

const createUser = z.object({ email: z.string().email(), name: z.string().min(1) })

app.post('/users', async (req, res) => {
  const body = createUser.parse(req.body)           // throws ZodError on bad input
  const user = await db.insertUser(body)            // a rejection reaches the error handler
  res.status(201).json(user)
})

app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ error: 'not_found' }))

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {                  // four arguments: error handler
  if (err.name === 'ZodError') return res.status(422).json({ error: 'invalid', details: err.issues })
  console.error(err)
  res.status(500).json({ error: 'internal_error' })
})

app.listen(3000)
```
In Express 5, a rejected promise or thrown error in an async handler is forwarded to the error handler automatically. In Express 4 you needed `try/catch` with `next(err)` or a wrapper library.

## What changed in Express 5
| Area | Express 5 behavior |
|---|---|
| Async errors | Rejected promises go to the error handler |
| Wildcards | Use `/*splat` instead of `*`; optional segments are `{/:id}` |
| `req.query` | A read-only getter; the default parser is simple |
| Removed | `req.param()`, `res.send(status)`, `app.del()` and similar deprecated aliases |
| Node | 18 or newer |

## In real products
- Group routes with `express.Router()` per resource (users, orders) and mount them under `/v1`.
- Put cross-cutting concerns in middleware: request IDs, logging (pino), auth, tenant resolution.
- Validate at the edge with a schema library so handlers receive typed, trusted data.
- Expose a health endpoint such as `/healthz` for load balancers and orchestrators.

> [!pitfall] Order matters. Register body parsers and security middleware before routes, and the 404 handler and error handler last.
> [!pitfall] Behind a proxy or load balancer, forgetting trust proxy makes every client look like the same IP, so rate limiting blocks everyone at once.
> [!security] Never send err.stack or database error messages to clients. Log them server-side and return a generic message with a request ID.
q: How does Express know a function is an error handler?
It declares four parameters: (err, req, res, next).
What is the main behavior change for async handlers in Express 5?
A thrown error or rejected promise is forwarded to the error-handling middleware automatically.

node-event-loop.md:
## Why it exists
JavaScript runs on one thread, yet a Node server handles thousands of connections. It works because Node never waits: it hands slow work (network, disk, timers) to the operating system or a small thread pool, and runs your callback when the result is ready. The **event loop** is the scheduler that decides what runs next.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
Your code runs to completion on the main thread. Then the loop cycles through phases: **timers** (expired `setTimeout` callbacks), **poll** (I/O callbacks such as finished reads and incoming requests), **check** (`setImmediate` callbacks) and **close** callbacks. Between every callback Node drains two **microtask** queues: `process.nextTick` first, then promise callbacks (`.then` and `await`).

Under the hood **libuv** provides the loop and a thread pool (4 threads by default) used for file system work, DNS lookups, and some crypto and compression. Network sockets use the operating system's async mechanisms instead.

## Worked example
```js
console.log('sync')
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0)
setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'))
process.nextTick(() => console.log('nextTick'))
// prints: sync, nextTick, promise, then timeout and immediate
```
`sync` always prints first, then `nextTick`, then `promise`. From the main module the order of `timeout` and `immediate` is not guaranteed. Inside an I/O callback, `immediate` always runs first.

## In real products
Every request handler is a callback on this one thread, so **one slow synchronous operation delays every other request**.
```js
// blocks all users while the loop runs
app.get('/report', (req, res) => {
  const rows = hugeArray.map(expensiveTransform)   // CPU-bound
  res.json(rows)
})
```
Fixes, in order of preference: do the work in the database, stream it in chunks, move it to a **worker thread** or a job queue, or run more processes (cluster or containers).
```js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads'

function runInWorker(file, data) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const w = new Worker(file, { workerData: data })
    w.once('message', resolve)
    w.once('error', reject)
  })
}
```

## Trade-offs
| Workload | Good fit for the event loop? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| APIs, proxies, chat, streaming | Yes | Mostly waiting on I/O |
| Image or video processing, ML inference | No | CPU-bound; use workers or separate services |
| Many tiny synchronous calls | Yes | Cheap as long as each stays short |

> [!pitfall] Synchronous APIs like fs.readFileSync, crypto.pbkdf2Sync and large JSON.parse calls freeze the loop. Use the async versions on the request path.
> [!pitfall] An unhandled promise rejection crashes the process on modern Node versions. Handle errors, and add a process-level handler that logs and exits so your supervisor restarts it.
> [!tip] Measure loop health with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay(). Rising delay means something is blocking.
q: Why does a long synchronous loop in one handler slow down every other request?
All handlers run as callbacks on the single main thread, so nothing else runs until the loop returns to the event loop.
Which runs first, process.nextTick or a resolved promise callback?
process.nextTick; its queue is drained before the promise microtask queue.
Where does file system work run?
In libuv's thread pool, not on the main thread.

q: You added `app.use((err, req, res) => {...})` as your error handler but it never runs. Why?

Express (and our mini version) detects error handlers by the function having exactly four parameters `(err, req, res, next)`. With three parameters it is treated as a normal middleware, so it is skipped while an error is being forwarded.
A route is registered above `app.use(express.json())` and `req.body` is `undefined` inside it. Explain.
Middleware and routes run in registration order. The route answered before the body parser layer was reached, so nothing parsed the body. Register the parser above the routes that need it.
In Express 5, an `async` handler throws. What happens, and what still hangs the request even in Express 5?

The rejected promise is forwarded to the error-handling middleware as `next(err)`. A handler that completes successfully but neither sends a response nor calls `next()` still leaves the request hanging, because resolved promises do not advance the chain.

node-streams.md:
## Why it exists
Reading a 2 GB file into memory before sending it crashes servers. **Streams** process data in small chunks as it arrives, so memory stays flat no matter how large the data is, and the first bytes reach the client immediately.

{{dg:0}}

## How it works
There are four kinds: **Readable** (a source), **Writable** (a destination), **Duplex** (both) and **Transform** (modifies data in between). `write()` returns `false` when the destination's buffer is full. That is **backpressure**, a signal to pause until the `drain` event. `pipeline` wires streams together and handles backpressure and cleanup for you.

## Worked example
```js
import { createReadStream } from 'node:fs'
import { createGzip } from 'node:zlib'
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises'

app.get('/export.csv.gz', async (req, res) => {
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/gzip')
  await pipeline(createReadStream('export.csv'), createGzip(), res)
})
```
Memory use stays at a few chunks (about 64 KB each for file streams) even for a multi-gigabyte file.

## In real products
- Streaming database results into a CSV download with a cursor.
- Proxying large uploads to object storage without buffering them.
- Streaming LLM tokens to the browser with Server-Sent Events.
- Web Streams (`ReadableStream`, `fetch` bodies) are the standards-based counterpart, and Node can convert between the two.

## Trade-offs
| Approach | Memory | Time to first byte | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read everything, then send | High | High | Low |
| Streams with pipeline | Low | Low | Medium |
| Manual .pipe() chains | Low | Low | Higher: easy to get error handling wrong |

> [!pitfall] readable.pipe(writable) does not forward errors or clean up on failure, which leaks file handles. Prefer pipeline from node:stream/promises.
> [!pitfall] Ignoring the return value of write() buffers unlimited data in memory when the client is slow.
> [!tip] The default highWaterMark is 16 KB for most streams and 64 KB for fs streams. Tune it only after measuring.
q: What does write() returning false mean?
The destination's internal buffer is full; pause writing until the drain event.
Why prefer pipeline over pipe?
pipeline propagates errors and destroys all streams on failure, preventing leaks.

q: Why is `Cart` easier to test when its price lookup is passed to the constructor than when it imports a network client directly?
The test can inject a fake (`mock.fn`) that returns canned prices, throws errors or counts calls, making the test fast, deterministic and independent of the network. This is dependency injection.
An async test calls `cart.total()` without `await` and asserts after. It always passes, even when the code is wrong. Why?

The test function returns before the promise settles, so the runner marks it passed and the assertion runs later (or never). Always `await` the call (or return the promise) and use `assert.rejects` for expected failures.
How does `node --test` tell your CI pipeline that tests failed, and how do you test code that uses `setTimeout(fn, 300)` without waiting 300 ms?

The runner exits with a non-zero status (1) when any test fails, and 0 when all pass. Use fake timers (`t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout'] })` and `tick(ms)`) so time advances instantly in the test.
